title: Calories Burned Household Chores 2026 | Hacé Cuentas
h1: How Many Calories Do Household Chores Burn?
description: Calculate calories burned doing household chores by weight, task & duration. MET-based data from Ainsworth's Compendium of Physical Activities.
seoKeywords: how many calories does housework burn
intro: Every vacuum session, bathroom scrub, or weekend yard cleanup burns real calories—yet most fitness trackers ignore them. According to the **U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics American Time Use Survey**, the average American spends over 2 hours/day on household chores, making them one of the largest untracked sources of daily physical activity. This calculator uses MET values from the **Compendium of Physical Activities** (Ainsworth et al., maintained at Arizona State University) — the gold standard cited by the **CDC** and **ACSM** for energy expenditure estimates. Formula: **Calories = MET × weight (kg) × duration (hours)**. Personalized to your weight, not a generic 70 kg reference.
keyTakeaway: **2 hours of household cleaning burns 200–400 calories** for most US adults, per the Compendium of Physical Activities and CDC physical activity guidelines. Gardening (MET 5.0) burns the most; ironing (MET 1.8) the least.

useCases.description: You skipped the gym but spent 90 minutes cleaning the apartment—vacuuming (30 min), mopping (30 min), and scrubbing the bathroom (30 min). At 75 kg, that's roughly: (3.3 × 75 × 0.5) + (3.5 × 75 × 0.5) + (3.5 × 75 × 0.5) = 123.75 + 131.25 + 131.25 = **386 calories burned**. Enough to close most activity goals without stepping outside.

useCases.title: Logging NEAT in a calorie-deficit plan
useCases.description: A 68 kg person on a 1,800 kcal/day deficit wants to account for every calorie out. They cook dinner 7 nights a week (45 min each, MET 2.5): 2.5 × 68 × 0.75 × 7 = **893 calories per week** from cooking alone—nearly 130 kcal/day that many diet apps miss entirely when set to 'sedentary.'

useCases.title: Comparing chores by calorie burn before choosing
useCases.description: A 80 kg homeowner has 60 minutes to spare and wants to maximize calorie burn. Vacuuming for 60 min = 3.3 × 80 × 1 = 264 kcal. Mowing the lawn (push mower, MET 5.5) for 60 min = 5.5 × 80 × 1 = **440 kcal**. Gardening (digging, MET 5.0) = 400 kcal. Clear winner: mowing the lawn burns 67% more than vacuuming in the same time.

useCases.title: Understanding why you feel tired after a big clean
useCases.description: A 65 kg person deep-cleans a 3-bedroom house over 4 hours: mixing vacuuming, mopping, scrubbing, and carrying laundry (average MET ~3.5). Total burn: 3.5 × 65 × 4 = **910 calories**—equivalent to running approximately 14 km at moderate pace. The fatigue is completely justified.

useCases.title: Justifying housework as cardio to a skeptical partner
useCases.description: A 72 kg person does 2 hours of yard work every Sunday: raking (MET 3.0) for 30 min + digging (MET 5.0) for 45 min + hauling bags (MET 4.0) for 45 min = (3.0×72×0.5) + (5.0×72×0.75) + (4.0×72×0.75) = 108 + 270 + 216 = **594 calories**. That's more than most 45-minute spin classes. Argument won.

useCases.title: Estimating weekly NEAT contribution for a stay-at-home parent
useCases.description: A 78 kg stay-at-home parent runs a household daily: cooking (45 min, MET 2.5) + dishwashing (20 min, MET 2.2) + vacuuming (20 min, MET 3.3) + laundry/folding (15 min, MET 2.0) = roughly 250 kcal/day × 7 days = **~1,750 kcal/week** from chores. This shifts their effective activity multiplier closer to 'lightly active' even without formal exercise.

useCases.title: Post-holiday calorie offset strategy
useCases.description: After Thanksgiving, a 85 kg person wants to offset 500 extra calories without a gym session. Mopping floors (MET 3.5) for 60 min = 297.5 kcal. Adding 45 min of yard cleanup (MET 4.0) = 255 kcal. Total: **552.5 kcal**—mission accomplished with a clean house as the bonus outcome.

useCases.title: Older adult tracking light activity for health monitoring
useCases.description: A 70-year-old weighing 67 kg can't do high-impact exercise but does household chores daily. Washing dishes (30 min, MET 2.2) + light tidying (30 min, MET 2.5) + slow gardening (30 min, MET 3.5) = (2.2×67×0.5) + (2.5×67×0.5) + (3.5×67×0.5) = 73.7 + 83.75 + 117.25 = **274.7 kcal/day**. Tracking this helps their doctor assess real daily energy expenditure.

explanation:
## METs by Household Chore

The **MET (Metabolic Equivalent)** measures energy intensity. 1 MET = sitting quietly.

| Chore | MET | Intensity | kcal/hour (70 kg) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ironing | 1.8 | Very light | 126 |
| Cooking | 2.0 | Light | 140 |
| Washing dishes | 2.2 | Light | 154 |
| Sweeping | 3.0 | Moderate low | 210 |
| Vacuuming | 3.3 | Moderate | 231 |
| Mopping / Wet cleaning | 3.5 | Moderate | 245 |
| Gardening | 5.0 | Moderate high | 350 |

### Formula

```
Calories = MET × weight (kg) × duration (hours)
```

### Comparison with Exercise

- **Vacuuming for 30 min** (MET 3.3) ≈ 30-minute easy walk
- **Gardening for 60 min** (MET 5.0) ≈ 60-minute casual bike ride
- **Cleaning your whole house for 2 hrs** (average MET 3.0) ≈ 250–350 calories

### The NEAT Concept

Household chores are part of **NEAT (Non-Exercise Activity Thermogenesis)**—all the calories you burn through daily movement that isn't formal exercise. NEAT can represent **200–900 calories/day** and is one of the key differences between people who maintain their weight and those who don't.

### Tips to Maximize Calorie Burn

- Turn on music and add rhythm to your cleaning.
- Go up and down the stairs when putting things away.
- Clean windows and high surfaces (uses more muscles).
- Do multiple chores in a row without sitting down.

faq.q: Does household chore activity count toward the WHO's recommended 150 minutes of weekly exercise?
faq.a: Partially, yes. The **WHO Global Guidelines on Physical Activity (2020)** state that moderate-intensity activities of any kind—including domestic and occupational work—contribute to the 150–300 minute weekly target. Chores like vacuuming (MET 3.3), mopping (MET 3.5), and gardening (MET 4.0–5.0) all qualify as moderate-intensity by the standard definition (MET 3.0–6.0). However, the guidelines also emphasize muscle-strengthening activities twice per week, which most household chores don't adequately cover. Think of chores as a solid foundation that counts toward your cardio minutes, not a complete fitness replacement. If you do 45 minutes of vigorous gardening three times a week, that's 135 minutes of moderate-equivalent activity—almost your full weekly target from yard work alone.

faq.q: Why does the formula use body weight? Shouldn't effort matter more?
faq.a: Body weight is the dominant variable in MET-based calorie calculations because **moving a heavier body requires more muscular work and cardiovascular output**—even for identical movements. A 90 kg person vacuuming exerts more force, elevates heart rate higher, and burns proportionally more energy than a 60 kg person making the same exact strokes. Effort (intensity) is captured by the MET value itself—a high MET means the task is inherently demanding regardless of who does it. The formula Calories = MET × weight (kg) × hours combines both: MET accounts for task intensity, weight accounts for individual metabolic cost. Fitness level, age, and muscle mass do influence efficiency slightly, but weight remains the single most accurate readily available predictor, which is why every major exercise science protocol uses it.

faq.q: Which specific chores burn the most calories per hour?
faq.a: Ranked by MET value from the Ainsworth Compendium: **1) Mowing lawn (push mower): MET 5.5** — 385 kcal/hr at 70 kg. **2) Digging/spading garden: MET 5.0** — 350 kcal/hr. **3) Carrying groceries upstairs: MET 4.5** — 315 kcal/hr. **4) Raking leaves: MET 3.8** — 266 kcal/hr. **5) Mopping/scrubbing floors: MET 3.5** — 245 kcal/hr. **6) Vacuuming: MET 3.3** — 231 kcal/hr. **7) Washing car by hand: MET 3.0** — 210 kcal/hr. **8) Cooking actively: MET 2.5** — 175 kcal/hr. **9) Washing dishes (standing): MET 2.2** — 154 kcal/hr. **10) Ironing: MET 1.8** — 126 kcal/hr. The pattern is clear: outdoor and floor-level tasks that engage large muscle groups top the list.

faq.q: How accurate are MET-based calorie estimates compared to a heart rate monitor or fitness tracker?
faq.a: MET formulas and wearable devices each have error ranges, and neither is perfectly accurate. **MET-based calculations** typically fall within ±15–20% of measured oxygen consumption in lab settings, per research published in the *Journal of Physical Activity and Health*. They tend to underestimate for very fit individuals (whose bodies are efficient) and overestimate for beginners. **Wearable fitness trackers** add heart rate data, which improves accuracy during rhythmic aerobic exercise—but household chores involve frequent stops, position changes, and mixed muscle groups that confuse optical heart rate sensors. Studies show trackers can be off by 20–30% for non-steady-state activities like cleaning. For most practical purposes—logging NEAT, estimating weekly burn, comparing tasks—MET estimates are entirely fit for purpose and scientifically defensible.

faq.q: What is NEAT, and how significant is housework in my total daily energy expenditure?
faq.a: **NEAT (Non-Exercise Activity Thermogenesis)** is all the energy you burn through movement that isn't formal exercise or sleeping—walking to your car, fidgeting, and yes, doing chores. According to research by Dr. James Levine at the Mayo Clinic, NEAT can account for **100 to 800 calories per day** depending on lifestyle, making it the most variable component of total daily energy expenditure (TDEE). For sedentary office workers, NEAT may be as low as 15% of TDEE. For someone who works a physical job or actively manages a home, it can reach 50%. Household chores are a primary NEAT driver. A person who cleans, cooks, and gardens daily without formal exercise can have a meaningfully higher TDEE than a gym-goer who sits the rest of the day—a phenomenon sometimes called the 'active couch potato' paradox in reverse.

faq.q: Does cleaning faster or more vigorously burn significantly more calories?
faq.a: Yes—intensity matters, and the Compendium captures this with separate MET values for different effort levels. For example, **general cleaning (MET 3.0)** vs. **vigorous scrubbing (MET 3.8)** represents a 27% difference in calorie burn for the same time. Similarly, slow gardening (MET 3.5) vs. heavy digging (MET 5.0) is a 43% gap. In practice, moving faster between tasks, scrubbing harder, carrying heavier loads, and minimizing rest time all elevate your effective MET. If you deliberately clean with intensity—fast-paced, minimal breaks, using full range of motion—you can push vacuuming closer to a MET of 4.0 rather than 3.3. It won't transform housework into a sprint session, but it meaningfully increases caloric output and cardiovascular benefit over the same duration.

faq.q: Can I log household chores in MyFitnessPal, Apple Health, or Garmin Connect?
faq.a: Yes, all three platforms support manual activity logging for household chores, though the level of granularity varies. **MyFitnessPal** has a dedicated 'Household/Cleaning' activity category with separate entries for vacuuming, mowing, gardening, and cooking. **Apple Health** accepts any workout type you manually add, including 'Other' with custom duration and calories—use this calculator's output to fill in the calorie field accurately. **Garmin Connect** allows manual activity entries where you input duration and calories burned. The key advantage of using this calculator first is getting a weight-accurate number rather than relying on the app's fixed-weight assumptions, which are often based on a generic 70–80 kg reference person. Enter your actual calculated calories as the activity energy for the most accurate TDEE tracking.

faq.q: Do household chores burn enough calories to support weight loss?
faq.a: They can meaningfully contribute—but context matters. A **500-calorie daily deficit** is the conventional target for losing approximately 0.45 kg (1 lb) per week. A 75 kg person doing 2 hours of mixed moderate-intensity chores burns roughly 400–500 kcal, which could theoretically cover most of that deficit on active cleaning days. However, research consistently shows that increasing activity often triggers compensatory behaviors—eating slightly more, resting slightly longer—that partially offset the extra burn. Chores are most effective for weight management when combined with dietary awareness rather than used as a standalone strategy. That said, for people who dislike structured exercise, committing to active daily housekeeping is a legitimate, sustainable way to increase weekly energy expenditure by 1,500–3,000 kcal without setting foot in a gym.

faq.q: Does the calorie burn from chores change as I lose weight?
faq.a: Yes, directly and proportionally. Since the formula is **Calories = MET × weight × hours**, a 10% drop in body weight produces a 10% drop in calories burned doing the same chore for the same duration. This is one reason weight loss tends to slow over time—your body becomes lighter and therefore burns fewer calories per unit of movement. For example, vacuuming for 30 minutes at 90 kg burns 148 kcal; at 75 kg (after losing 15 kg) the same session burns only 124 kcal—a 16% reduction. Practically speaking, you'd need to either increase duration, choose higher-MET chores, or add other activity to maintain the same caloric contribution as you lose weight. Re-running this calculator every 5–10 kg of weight change will keep your estimates current.

faq.q: Are calorie estimates different for older adults or people with physical limitations?
faq.a: The MET formula doesn't adjust for age directly, but **older adults and people with physical limitations often have lower actual energy expenditure** than the formula predicts—for two reasons. First, reduced muscle mass (sarcopenia) lowers basal metabolic rate, meaning the 'resting' baseline embedded in the MET calculation is already lower. Second, movement efficiency tends to decrease with age and some disabilities, meaning more perceived effort but not necessarily more caloric output. Conversely, people who are deconditioned may actually burn *more* than predicted because the same task represents a higher relative intensity for their cardiovascular system. For older adults tracking health rather than weight loss, the MET estimates remain useful as relative comparisons between activities, even if absolute accuracy varies. Always cross-reference with a physician's guidance if chores are being used to meet specific medical activity targets.

faq.q: What's the difference between gross and net calories burned, and which does this calculator show?
faq.a: **Gross calories** include everything your body burns during an activity—both the calories needed for the movement itself and the calories you'd have burned anyway just being alive (your resting metabolic rate, or RMR). **Net calories** subtract the RMR portion and represent only the additional burn attributable to the activity. The standard MET formula (MET × weight × hours) calculates **gross calories**, which is what this calculator displays—and what most fitness apps and food logging tools use for consistency. If you need net calories (some research protocols and certain apps request this), subtract approximately 1.0 MET worth of energy: Net kcal = (MET − 1.0) × weight (kg) × hours. For a 70 kg person vacuuming for 1 hour: Gross = 231 kcal, Net = 161 kcal. The difference matters most for precise calorie-in/calorie-out accounting but is minor for general wellness tracking.

faq.q: How do household chores compare to common gym exercises in calorie burn?
faq.a: The comparison is more favorable to chores than most people expect. **Vigorous gardening (MET 5.0)** matches casual cycling on a stationary bike (MET 5.5). **Mopping floors (MET 3.5)** is equivalent to a leisurely swim (MET 3.5). **Vacuuming (MET 3.3)** mirrors a 20-min/mile walking pace (MET 3.0–3.5). Where gym exercise pulls ahead is in **duration consistency and progressive overload**—you can sustain a treadmill session at a fixed intensity for 45 minutes more reliably than the mixed-effort pattern of cleaning. Gym workouts also produce superior strength and cardiovascular adaptation because they're structured. The practical takeaway: chores and gym sessions aren't competing categories. On gym days, chores add bonus NEAT. On rest days, chores keep your metabolism ticking. The combination—active lifestyle plus structured exercise—produces better outcomes than either alone.
